topic: Three numbers on a scrap of paper
text:
Ok so if you're starting over after a divorce and your money brain is just static, do this today. Grab a scrap of paper and write down what comes in each month, what goes out, and how many months you could keep going on what you have. Three numbers, that's it. There's a free one-page sheet if you want it to look nice, link in bio.

Day one counts.

Open your bank app, scroll back thirty days, and say the total that came in out loud. To the cat, to the car, whoever's listening. It feels so weird lol, but if you're rebuilding after a divorce that one number is a really good place to stand. The free Starter Sheet has a spot for it, link in bio.

Day one counts.

Quick question for anyone starting over: if nothing changed at all, how many months could you keep going? Take what you've got, divide it by a normal month of spending, and round it. Could be two months, could be twenty. Either way you finally have a number instead of a vibe. The free sheet at the link in bio walks you through it.

Day one counts.

Everybody has a drawer or a folder of statements they've been dodging, ngl. Pull out just the newest one and read what came in and what went out. That's all you're doing today. It's a way gentler start than a full budget, especially if you're rebuilding after a divorce. The free Three Numbers Starter Sheet is at the link in bio.

Day one counts.

Hot take for anyone starting over with money: start your list with what you're keeping. The good coffee, the standing lunch with a friend, the gym that actually gets you out the door. Protect those first and look at everything else after. What's on your keep list right now?

A money plan with zero fun in it gets abandoned by month two, tbh. Pick two or three things you're keeping on purpose, like a weekly walk or pizza night, especially if you're rebuilding after a divorce and everything feels up for review. You chose them, so go ahead and say so. What's on yours?

Ten minute thing for tonight, grab a pen. Write down five things you spend money on that you'd really miss if they vanished, then circle the two you'd miss most. Those two get protected first while you rebuild, and everything else can wait. Which two did you circle?

You're allowed to want nice things while you rebuild. New sheets, a good candle, the fancy olive oil. After a divorce especially, that can be a real line in your budget when you put it there on purpose. Follow along if you want one small money step a day. What's the nice thing on your list?

If money feels tighter than it should after a divorce, go hunting for the little leaks. The gym you quit going to, the streaming thing nobody watches, the free trial that quietly turned into a monthly charge lol. Scroll back a month and circle anything you don't recognize. Part 2 of the $17 Day Zero Workbook, Where It Went, walks you through it. Link in bio.

Day one counts.

Canceling something or asking for a lower bill is the phone call everyone puts off for weeks. So the $17 Day Zero Workbook has Dreaded Call Scripts, actual words you can read out loud while you're on hold. Pick the one call you've been avoiding and put it on your calendar for this week. Link in bio.

Day one counts.

Autopay is amazing right up until you realize you can't name half the things on it. Take twenty minutes with a blank page and write down everything that pulls money out without asking you first. I bet there's one you can pause. The Year-at-a-Glance Bill Tracker in the $17 Day Zero Workbook gives that list a home. Link in bio.

Day one counts.

My order is Keep, Cut, Earn, Build, and Cut sits second on purpose, because the first job is deciding what's worth protecting. After that, trimming feels way lighter. The whole method is in the 32-page Day Zero Workbook, $17, written for women rebuilding after a divorce. Link in bio.

Day one counts.

Think about the last few times someone asked you for help with something. A spreadsheet, a resume, a form that made no sense. Those little favors are a decent clue about what you could offer for a fair price someday, and you don't have to quit anything to find out. What do people always ask you for help with?

If all you had was a phone or a laptop, what could you do this month that somebody might pay a fair price for? Proofreading, organizing a closet, setting up a friend's budget spreadsheet. Pick one and stick it on a sticky note where you'll see it. Follow along for one small money step a day. What's your idea?

Before you add any side income, count the hours. Five extra hours a week have to come from somewhere, and if you're coming out of a divorce your calendar might already be stuffed with appointments, errands and sleep you're trying to catch up on. Pull up your real week and look at it. What would you drop to make room?

Your resume is probably underselling you. Writing, organizing, teaching, fixing things, staying calm when a form is due tomorrow all count. Set a timer, write ten skills without editing, then circle the one you like most. What's number one on your page?

A good first hour for your money is pretty unglamorous. List every account with your name on it, write down each bill and its due date, and change any password you've been reusing. Boring, yes, but everything else sits on top of it. Part 4 of the $17 Day Zero Workbook, The First Hour, walks through it. Link in bio.

Day one counts.

Some days you've got fifteen minutes and zero energy. There's a bonus in the $17 Day Zero Workbook called the Fifteen-Minute Start that's built for exactly those days. Rebuilding after a divorce adds up slowly, one finished small thing at a time, and a small thing still counts. Link in bio.

Day one counts.

Rebuilding after a divorce feels a lot more doable when each week only has one job. Week one, a list of your accounts. Week two, a calendar of your bills. Week three, a small cushion, even if it's twenty bucks. The 32-page Day Zero Workbook, $17, lays out the order so you don't have to guess. Link in bio.

Day one counts.

Before you sit down with a lawyer, accountant or planner, write your questions out. Seriously, the meeting goes so much better. Questions for a Money Helper is a bonus page in the $17 Day Zero Workbook for exactly that. A licensed professional can help with the big stuff, and a page of questions gets you in the door ready. Link in bio.

Day one counts.

It's 2 A.M., you're doing money math in your head, and every number looks worse in the dark. Write the numbers on paper, close the notebook, and look again after coffee. They almost always look smaller on paper in the morning than they did in your head at night. Who else has done the 2 A.M. math?

Next time your brain starts in on how did I let this happen, try asking where did the money go, and open one statement to find out. A highlighter and ten minutes gets you most of the way. Circle the three biggest charges, then circle anything you don't recognize. Save this one for when you need it.

Day one counts.

Nobody feels ready to start over with money, and the first week is usually a little clumsy lol. Give yourself one small task, like finding the login to your own bank account, and let that be the whole day. Zero is a starting line. Follow along and we'll keep the steps small. What's your small task this weekend?

Permission slip for this weekend: you can go slowly, you can do a rough first draft of your accounts list, and you can read the same page twice. Starting over at any age, from wherever you are, is allowed to be messy. Send this to a friend who could use it.

Day one counts.

The Monthly Twenty is a standing date with your own money. Twenty minutes, once a month, same chair, maybe a snack. Look at your three numbers, see what moved, and pick one small thing for the month ahead. If you're rebuilding after a divorce it gives the whole project a rhythm. The free Three Numbers Starter Sheet at the link in bio is a good place to write them.

Day one counts.

Your Sunday reset can fit inside one cup of tea. Open your bank app, look at the week, and write down one number you want to remember, maybe what you spent on groceries. Then close the app and go live your life. The free one-page Three Numbers Starter Sheet is at the link in bio if you want a place to keep the numbers.

Day one counts.

Once a month, ask yourself three things. What came in? What went out? How many months could I keep going if nothing changed? If the answers moved, now you know. If they stayed put, that's good info too. Write them on the free Three Numbers Starter Sheet, link in bio, and stick it in a drawer until next month.

Day one counts.

Put the Monthly Twenty on your calendar like a coffee date with a friend. Same day each month, short agenda, zero lectures. Money looks so much friendlier when you visit it regularly, especially in the year or two after a divorce. The free Starter Sheet makes the visit quick, and it's at the link in bio.

Day one counts.
